Batched bootstrap now plans and pushes the trunk first, plans every other branch in one commit-graph fetch, and pushes small branches in shared packs (ENT-3617).

## Problem

`planBatches` fetched each branch's commit graph with its own request, one at a time, and pushed nothing until every branch was planned. On a repository with thousands of branches, planning outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so every attempt timed out with nothing on the target and each retry started over.

## Change

- The trunk is planned and pushed first, so a timeout later in the sync keeps the default branch.
- The remaining branches share one `tree:0` commit-graph fetch (all tips as wants, trunk as have) instead of one request each.
- Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly. A group over the pack budget splits in half; a branch too big to share a pack keeps its own checkpointed batch.
- `FetchCommitParents` now takes its wants as a list of hashes.
- Test harness: the git-http-backend test server buffers chunked request bodies, which `net/http/cgi` rejects.

## Measurements

Against github.com/openclaw/openclaw (3,904 branches), from a laptop:

- Before (v0.10.0, per-branch fetch): ~450 ms per branch request, ~25 minutes of planning.
- After: one fetch with 3,904 wants and the trunk as have returned 21,831 commits in 19.5 s, no error. GitHub accepts the large want list.

## Tests

`go test ./internal/strategy/bootstrap/ ./internal/gitproto/ ./internal/syncer/` passes.

==== d851ee02 2026-04-15 Plan trunk first in batched bootstrap to cut per-branch graph fetches
Before: each branch's checkpoint planning fetched the full commit graph
from the source independently. For a repo with 152 feature branches that
all descend from main, that meant ~152 full-history commit-graph fetches
and ~152 independent first-parent walks, each traversing the same shared
history. On a linux-sized source this was ~40 s of wall time during
planning alone, before any object bytes moved.

Now the trunk is identified up front via the source's HEAD symref, planned
first, and its commit reachability is captured as a hash set. Each
subsequent branch's graph fetch passes trunk's tip as a have so the source
returns only the divergence, and the first-parent walk terminates when it
enters trunk's ancestry instead of walking back to root.

Pieces:

- gitproto: expose HEAD symref on RefService.HeadTarget. v1 reads it from
  the symref capability; v2 adds "symrefs" to ls-refs and a "ref-prefix
  HEAD" argument so HEAD is actually returned (otherwise ref-prefix
  refs/heads/ filters it out and HeadTarget stays empty). HEAD itself is
  consumed for the symref target and not surfaced in the ref slice,
  matching v1 behavior where symbolic refs are filtered downstream.
- gitproto: FetchCommitGraph takes an optional []plumbing.Hash of haves,
  forwarded into the v2 fetch command. Nil/empty preserves prior behavior.
- planner: add FirstParentChainStoppingAt that terminates the walk when a
  commit is in a caller-supplied stop set. FirstParentChain becomes a thin
  wrapper with nil stop set for existing callers.
- bootstrap: orderTrunkFirst reorders DesiredRefs so the HEAD branch is
  planned first; collectCommitHashes extracts just the commit hash set
  (~8 B per commit, ~11 MB for linux) from trunk's graph store before it
  is GC'd. Subsequent branches plan with trunk's tip as a have and
  trunk's ancestry as a stop set. Emits one of three diagnostic log lines
  at planning time so operators can see whether the fast path fired:
  trunk selected, trunk unset (no HEAD advertised), or trunk unset (HEAD
  filtered by --branch/--map). Subsumed branches (tip in trunk's
  ancestry) emit a single-checkpoint batch today — the pack push for
  those is a follow-up optimization.

Empty-chain edge case: when stop-at subsumes the branch tip,
FirstParentChainStoppingAt returns nil and planCheckpointsFromChain
==== fc37c094 2026-04-15 Skip pack push for branches fully subsumed by trunk
When trunk is planned first, its ancestry set already tells us which
branches contain no new commits — their tip is already reachable from
trunk, so trunk's batches have delivered every object those branches
need. Previously those branches still ran the full checkpoint machinery:
a commit-graph fetch (usually near-empty), a pack fetch (usually
near-empty), a temp-ref push, a cutover push, and a temp-ref delete.

With this change, the subsumed case is detected in planBatches before the
commit-graph fetch, and the resulting plannedBatch carries a subsumed
flag instead of checkpoints. executeBatched handles that flag with a
single ref-create PushCommand that points at the source hash — no fetch,
no pack, no temp ref, no cutover dance.

Correctness rests on trunkStopSet containing every commit reachable from
the trunk tip, not just the first-parent chain. collectCommitHashes
iterates all CommitObjects in the tree:0 fetch result, so merges and
their ancestors are included. A branch tip is therefore only marked
subsumed when its entire history is already covered by trunk's batches.

Added TestExecuteBatchedSubsumedBranchSkipsPack verifies that for a
feature branch pointing at an older commit on trunk's chain, the planner
emits zero commit-graph fetches and zero pack fetches for that branch,
and the executor issues only a single ref-create via PushCommands.

Webhook-count note: GitHub fires one push event per ref update, so the
subsumed branch still generates one webhook when its ref is created.
This change cuts the per-branch HTTP round-trips and object transfer for
that branch, not the webhook event itself. Operators concerned about
webhook volume during bulk migrations should still disable target
webhooks for the duration of the run.

Your trunk-first work was in **bootstrap**, not replicate. Replicate has no trunk or HEAD ordering at all. PR #130 builds on your logic rather than duplicating it.

**What you built earlier (all in `internal/strategy/bootstrap`)**
- `d851ee02` (Apr 15), "Plan trunk first in batched bootstrap": `orderTrunkFirst` puts the source HEAD branch first in planning. The trunk's ancestry becomes a stop set, and its tip is sent as a `have` when fetching each other branch's commit graph. That way each branch fetch returns only where it differs from the trunk.
- `fc37c094` (Apr 15), "Skip pack push for branches fully subsumed by trunk": if a branch's tip is already in the trunk's history, bootstrap just creates the ref. No fetch, no pack.
- `e5dd3bac` / `833b123c` (May 12): bootstrap sends the source HEAD branch's push first, so GitHub and GitLab pick the right default branch.

**Why that wasn't enough for the incident repo (ENT-3617, PR #130 by Andrea, merged last night)**

Your version planned the trunk first, but `planBatches` still had to plan *every* branch before pushing anything. Each non-subsumed branch also got its own commit-graph request, one after another. The `have` made each response small, but every request still took about 450 ms. With about 3,900 branches, planning alone took about 25 minutes. That ran past the 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt ended with nothing on the target and the retry started over. Your tests with many refs most likely stayed below that point: in your commit message, 152 branches took about 40 s of planning.

**What #130 changed**
1. **The trunk is pushed before anything else is planned.** Other branches are planned in `planAfterTrunk`, so a timeout later in the sync still leaves the default branch on the target.
2. **One commit-graph fetch for all remaining branches**, with all tips as `wants` and the trunk as the `have`, instead of one request per branch. Against openclaw (3,904 branches) that took 19.5 s.
3. **Small branches share packs** (`branch_group.go`): one fetch and one push create many refs directly, without temp refs. A group that's over budget splits. A branch too big to share a pack keeps the old per-branch checkpoint path.
4. Follow-ups:
   - When the target rejects a group push, the shared pack budget and the target's announced size limit are updated.
   - Large shared histories are pushed first, so later pushes can send them as `haves`.
   - Failed group pushes record which refs they already created, so the retry skips them.

Partly. The regression that caused the incident is covered by unit tests that run in CI. The new integration test passes, but it never runs automatically.

**Unit tests (run in CI via `mise run test:ci`)**

These are in `internal/strategy/bootstrap/branch_group_test.go` and use a fake source and target that record every fetch and push.
- `TestExecuteBatchedGroupsSmallBranchesInOnePush` is the real guard against the incident bug. It checks that there are exactly 2 commit-graph fetches: the trunk, then all branches together. If anyone brings back one fetch per branch, it fails.
- `TestExecuteBatchedPushesTrunkBeforePlanningOtherBranches` checks the exact order: trunk graph, trunk push, one graph fetch for the other branches, one group push. That guards "the trunk lands before the rest is planned".
- Other tests cover:
  - oversized groups splitting
  - a single oversized branch, or one with a resume marker, running on its own
  - learning the target's size limit
  - not re-pushing refs that already landed
  - splitting when the source's pack is too large

**Integration test: real `git http-backend`, not run in CI**

`TestBootstrap_GitHTTPBackendBatchedManyBranches` (`internal/syncer/git_http_backend_test.go`) builds a source with:
- a trunk
- 30 small branches
- 2 branches already merged into the trunk
- one large branch
- a tag

All the chunking is in **bootstrap**. Replicate has none.

**Bootstrap** (`internal/strategy/bootstrap/`) has all of it:
- splitting a branch's history into checkpoints and subdividing them when a pack is too big
- the pack budget, learning the target's size limit, and fallback budgets
- since #130, the branch groups in `branch_group.go`: grouping small branches, splitting groups that are over budget, and giving a branch that's too big its own checkpointed batch

**Replicate** (`internal/strategy/replicate/replicate.go`) fetches **one pack** for everything that changed and relays it in one push. `MaxPackBytes` is only a hard cap (`gitproto.LimitPackReader`, line 67): over the limit the run fails, it doesn't split. Incremental works the same way.

**How a replicate run gets to the chunking**

`runReplicate` calls `replicateBootstrapRoute` (`internal/syncer/syncer.go:1261`). That hands the run to bootstrap only if **every** desired ref is missing on the target, and also either:
- prune wouldn't delete anything in scope, or
- a bootstrap resume marker (a temp ref) exists for one of the desired branches.

A first mirror into an empty repo therefore goes through bootstrap and gets the chunking. Once any desired ref exists on the target, the run uses plain replicate with one pack.

**A possible gap after #130 (I haven't tested this)**

#130 pushes the trunk first, and group pushes create the real refs directly. Say a run like the incident one times out after the trunk and some groups have landed. On the next run, `desiredTargetRefsAbsent` is false, so the resume-marker check never runs either. That run goes to plain replicate and tries to move the remaining several thousand branches in one pack, with no chunking. Depending on the size, that hits `MaxPackBytes` or the target's body limit, or it runs past the sync budget again.

Before #130 the same thing could already happen once any per-branch batch had cut over, but now it's the expected outcome of a timeout. Whether it matters depends on how big the leftover branches' pack is. For openclaw, branches unique to their own commits may be small enough to fit.

It's a real gap. The new test reproduces it: once the trunk is already on the target, every following replicate run fails, and nothing ever changes that.

**The test:** `TestReplicate_GitHTTPBackendResumeAfterTrunkLanded` in `internal/syncer/git_http_backend_test.go`. It uses the same settings as the mirror-pipeline worker: replicate, `Prune`, `IncludeTags`, and no configured pack limit. To act like a hosted target, I gave the test `git http-backend` server a request body limit: receive-pack POSTs over 1 MB get a 413. The source has a trunk of about 450 KB plus 20 branches, each with about 120 KB of its own data. It runs two cases:

| Target before the run | Path taken | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Empty | `bootstrap-batch` (reason `empty-target-managed-refs`) | **Passes.** The first push gets the 413, bootstrap switches to batched mode, and 21 refs land in 7 batches. |
| Trunk only (what a run that timed out after the trunk leaves) | plain replicate | **Fails.** `replicate relay failed: … http 413 … request body too large`. Nothing is pushed. |

**Why it gets stuck**
- `replicateBootstrapRoute` sends a run to bootstrap only if every desired ref is missing on the target. One ref already there, like the trunk, is enough to send the run down plain replicate.
- The resume-marker check sits behind that same condition, so a bootstrap temp ref wouldn't route the run to bootstrap either.
- Plain replicate puts all the missing branches in one pack, and it has no way to recover from the target's 413. Bootstrap does (the "switching to batched mode" line in the passing case).
- Each retry therefore sends the same oversized pack and gets the same 413.

On a repo the size of the incident one, the next run after a timeout would hit the body limit and never finish. #130 makes this the expected outcome of a timeout, because it lands the trunk early by design. The gap itself is older: any per-branch batch that had already cut over before a timeout caused the same thing.

**Possible fixes**
1. **(Recommended)** When replicate gets a body-limit error and the plan is only creates, fall back to batched bootstrap for the missing refs, using the target's existing refs as haves. That matches what the empty-target path already does.
2. Widen `replicateBootstrapRoute` so that "only creates, many refs missing" goes to bootstrap up front. That avoids one wasted push but is a heuristic.

- `git_http_backend_test.go` has the test server's `maxPushBody` limit and the new test. The "trunk already on target" case is deliberately left failing until the fix lands.

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.
- SSH fetches from GitHub intermittently failed with `update object storage: empty packfile`. The SSH transport wrote the request and closed stdin while the server was still streaming its ref advertisement (36 MB for `NixOS/nixpkgs`), and GitHub sometimes dropped a request that arrived that early. The request is now sent only after the advertisement is read, which is what `git` does. On the old code, 2 of 4 runs against `git@github.com:NixOS/nixpkgs.git` failed; with the change, 7 of 7 passed.
- Errors from closing an upload-pack stream (the ssh exit status and the remote's stderr) were dropped in `fetchToStoreV1` and `fetchToStoreV2`, because `CheckClose` wrote to a shadowed `err`. They are now joined into the returned error.

content.text:
I've built the fix: when a target refuses replicate's single pack, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap instead of failing on every retry. The integration test that failed before now passes. Nothing is committed yet.

**What changed**
- **Replicate falls back to batched bootstrap** (`internal/syncer/syncer.go`). It triggers when replicate's push fails with a body-limit or push-deadline error, the source supports batched bootstrap, and the run creates at least one ref. It then:
  1. re-reads the target's refs, because a push that hit a deadline may have applied some of them;
  2. creates the still-missing refs with batched bootstrap;
  3. pushes the remaining updates and deletes as a separate replicate push.

  Such a run reports relay mode `bootstrap-batch` with the new reason `replicate-pack-rejected`. The mirror-pipeline doesn't read the relay fields, so nothing changes on its side.
- **Bootstrap gets a `RejectedPush` param**, so it starts directly in batched mode rather than re-sending the pack the target just refused. The "switch to batched" logic is now one helper shared with the existing one-shot path.
- **Bootstrap plans against refs already on the target.** When the trunk is already on the target, every branch is now planned in one commit-graph fetch, with the target's refs as haves. Branches whose history the target already has are created without sending a pack. Without this, every branch got its own fetch and its own checkpointed push (a mutation test confirmed that). Bootstrap resume markers are left out of the haves, so an interrupted branch still resumes instead of starting over.

**Tests**
- `TestRun_IntegrationReplicateBatchesMissingRefsAfterTargetBodyLimit` runs in CI, using the in-process server with a 300 KB body limit. It fails with the fallback turned off.
- `TestReplicate_GitHTTPBackendResumeAfterTrunkLanded` runs against real `git http-backend` with three starting states: empty target, trunk already on the target, and trunk one commit behind (so an update rides along with the creates). All three pass.
- New bootstrap unit tests cover planning against target refs, starting batched from a refused push, refusing a push error batching can't fix, and leaving resume markers out of the haves.
- `mise run test:ci` and `mise run lint` are both clean.

**Also changed**
- The `test:git-http-backend` mise task now includes the new test and #130's many-branches test.
- `CHANGELOG.md` has an entry under Fixed.

**Not fixed**
- **Two older gated tests fail:** `TestBootstrap_GitHTTPBackendBatchedBranch` and `…BranchResume`. They fail the same way on `main` and on the commit before #130. The old task pattern never ran them, so I left them out of the task rather than fix them here.
- **One wasted upload per affected run.** The fallback only starts after replicate's full-size push has been refused. With a deadline error, that's a full timeout first.
- **Large updates can still fail.** Updates and deletes still go out in one replicate pack, so a single update bigger than the target's limit fails as before.
- **Only replicate is covered.** The `sync` path has no such fallback; the mirror-pipeline only uses replicate.

You were right: they test the same mechanism. Both fail because packs get split at push time, which is exactly what my fallback relies on. But the failures were outdated assertions, not a bug, and they fail the same way on `main` without my changes.

**Why they failed**
- Both tests use a 350 KB pack budget with about 200 KB of random data per commit. Bootstrap plans checkpoints from a fixed size estimate per commit, which comes out much lower than that, so it plans 2 batches.
- When a pack is actually pushed, the client stops its own upload once the pack is projected to go over the budget, and splits it ("projected to exceed target limit — splitting 2 → 6 packs"). The run succeeds and the ref lands.
- The assertions assumed the up-front plan was exact:
  - **BatchedBranch** required batches run to equal batches planned (it ran 6, planned 2).
  - **BranchResume** required a resumed run to use fewer batches than the planned count of 2. It ran 3, which is still fewer than a full run's 6.
- `PlannedBatchCount` is only used for reporting: the result output and the bench tool. Nothing depends on it being exact.

I couldn't find when they last passed. On older commits these tests don't fail on assertions; they hang until the timeout, even with #130's harness fix applied. Before #130 the gated `git http-backend` tests couldn't run at all, and the mise task's pattern skipped these two anyway, so nobody noticed.

**What I changed**
- **BatchedBranch** now checks that the run executed at least the planned batches, rather than exactly that many.
- **BranchResume** now also runs a full bootstrap to a second, empty target and checks the resumed run used fewer batches than that. That's what the test was trying to show; before, it compared against the plan's estimate.
- The `test:git-http-backend` task now runs all of the `TestBootstrap_GitHTTPBackend*` tests and the new `TestReplicate_GitHTTPBackend*` test.

All 12 gated tests pass, and lint is clean. The scratch worktrees I made for this are removed. Nothing is committed yet.
